prompt: Which part of a cell controls the cell's activities and contains its genetic information?

options.text: Nucleus
Cell membrane
Cytoplasm
Vacuole

feedback.b: The cell membrane controls what goes in and out of the cell, not the cell's activities.
feedback.c: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance where many reactions happen.
feedback.d: The vacuole stores water and other substances.

hints: Think about where DNA is kept.
solution: The **nucleus** contains DNA, which carries the instructions that control the cell's activities.

prompt: Select **all** the structures found in plant cells but **not** in animal cells.

options.text: Cell wall
Chloroplast
Nucleus
Cell membrane
Large permanent vacuole

hints: Two of the options are found in every plant and animal cell.
Think about what a plant needs to do that an animal doesn't, such as photosynthesis and staying rigid.
solution: Plant cells have a **cell wall** (support), **chloroplasts** (photosynthesis) and a **large permanent vacuole** (stores water and keeps the cell firm). Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus and a cell membrane.

prompt: Match each cell part to its job.

right.text: Control what enters and leaves the cell

hints: Mitochondria are often called the cell's 'powerhouse'.
solution: Mitochondria → respiration; chloroplast → photosynthesis; cell membrane → controls what enters and leaves; cell wall → support.

prompt: Put these levels of organisation in order, from smallest to largest.
hints: A group of similar cells working together forms a tissue.
solution: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. For example: muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → human.

prompt: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece lens and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
hints: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
solution: Total magnification $= 10 \times 40 = 400$, so the image is **×400**.

prompt: Name the green structures in a leaf cell where photosynthesis happens.
hints: They contain the green pigment chlorophyll.
solution: **Chloroplasts.** They contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

prompt: Animal cells have a cell [[a]] but no cell [[b]], so they do not have a fixed shape.
hints: One of these structures is rigid and found only in plants (and some other organisms).
solution: Animal cells have a cell **membrane** but no cell **wall**. The rigid cell wall is what gives plant cells their fixed shape.

prompt: Root cells of a plant do not contain chloroplasts, but leaf cells do. Explain why.
modelAnswer: Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens, and photosynthesis needs light. Leaf cells are exposed to sunlight, so they have chloroplasts to absorb light energy and make glucose. Root cells are underground where there is no light, so chloroplasts would be no use to them.

rubric.criterion: States that chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis
Links this to roots being underground with no light, so chloroplasts aren't needed

hints: What do chloroplasts do, and what do they need to do it?
solution: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, which needs light energy. Leaves receive light; roots grow in the dark soil, so chloroplasts would have no light to use.

prompt: What is the basic unit (building block) that all living things are made of?
hints: Every living thing, from bacteria to a kauri tree, is made of one or more of these.
solution: The **cell** is the basic unit of life. Some organisms, such as bacteria, are just one cell. Your body is made of trillions of cells.

prompt: Which part of a light microscope do you look through?

options.text: Eyepiece lens
Objective lens
Stage
Diaphragm

feedback.b: The objective lenses sit just above the slide. You look through the eyepiece at the top.
feedback.c: The stage is the flat platform that holds the slide.
feedback.d: The diaphragm controls how much light passes up through the slide.

hints: It's the lens at the top of the microscope, closest to your eye.
solution: You look through the **eyepiece lens**. It usually magnifies ×10, and it works together with the objective lens to magnify the specimen.

prompt: Which set of structures is found in a human cheek cell?

options.text: Nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria
Nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and cell wall
Nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and chloroplasts
Cytoplasm, cell wall, large vacuole and chloroplasts

feedback.b: Cheek cells are animal cells, and animal cells have no cell wall.
feedback.c: Chloroplasts are only found in cells that photosynthesise, such as leaf cells. Cheek cells don't photosynthesise.
feedback.d: These are plant cell structures. A cheek cell has no cell wall, large vacuole or chloroplasts.

hints: A cheek cell is an animal cell.
Rule out any option that includes a structure found only in plant cells.
solution: A cheek cell is an animal cell, so it has a **nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria**. It has no cell wall, no chloroplasts and no large permanent vacuole.

prompt:
A microscope gives a total magnification of ×600 when the ×40 objective lens is used. What is the magnification of the eyepiece lens?

Enter the number only (for example, 10 for ×10).
hints: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
You know the total and the objective, so divide.
solution:
Eyepiece magnification $= 600 \div 40 = 15$, so the eyepiece is **×15**.

Check: $15 \times 40 = 600$ ✓

prompt: Put these steps for focusing a light microscope in the correct order.

items.text: Place the slide on the stage, with the lowest-power objective lens in position
Watching from the side, use the coarse focus to bring the lens close to the slide
Looking through the eyepiece, turn the coarse focus to move the lens and slide apart until the image appears
Use the fine focus to make the image sharp
Switch to a higher-power objective lens and refocus using only the fine focus

hints: Always start with the lowest-power objective lens.
Watch from the side while the lens moves towards the slide, so you don't crack the slide.
solution:
1. Slide on the stage, lowest-power objective in place.
2. Watching from the side, bring the lens close to the slide with the coarse focus.
3. Looking through the eyepiece, move the lens and slide apart with the coarse focus until the image appears.
4. Sharpen the image with the fine focus.
5. Change to a higher-power lens and use only the fine focus.

You only move the lens **away** from the slide while looking through the eyepiece, so you can't crash the lens into the slide.

prompt: Why do students add a drop of iodine solution to onion skin cells on a microscope slide?

options.text: To stain the cells so structures such as the nucleus are easier to see
To kill any bacteria that might be on the slide
To make the cells swell up so they are easier to see
To glue the cover slip firmly onto the slide

feedback.b: Killing bacteria isn't the reason. The stain is used to add colour and contrast.
feedback.c: The stain doesn't change the size of the cells. Magnification comes from the lenses.
feedback.d: The cover slip is held in place by the liquid underneath it, not by the stain.

hints: Onion skin cells are almost see-through.
solution: Onion cells are nearly transparent, so they are hard to see. Iodine is a **stain**: it colours parts of the cells, such as the nucleus and cell wall, so they show up clearly.

prompt: A plant cell wall is made of [[a]], which makes it strong. The large permanent vacuole is filled with [[b]], which pushes outwards and keeps the cell firm.
hints: The wall is made of a tough carbohydrate that also gives vegetables their fibre.
The liquid in the vacuole is a watery solution of sugars and salts.
solution: The cell wall is made of **cellulose**. The vacuole is filled with **cell sap**, a solution of water, sugars and salts. When the vacuole is full, it presses against the cell wall and keeps the cell firm.

prompt: Match each specialised cell to the feature that helps it do its job.

right.text: No nucleus, leaving more room to carry oxygen
Long, thin extension that gives a large surface area for absorbing water
A tail for swimming to the egg
Lots of mitochondria to release energy for movement

hints: Think about each cell's job first: carrying, absorbing, swimming, photosynthesising or moving.
solution: Red blood cell → no nucleus (more room for oxygen); root hair cell → long extension (large surface area); sperm cell → tail; palisade cell → many chloroplasts; muscle cell → many mitochondria (energy for contracting).

prompt: Hemi is looking at onion cells through the ×4 objective lens. He switches to the ×40 objective lens and refocuses. What will he notice?

options.text: The cells look bigger, but he can see fewer of them
The cells look smaller, and he can see more of them
The cells look the same size, but they are sharper
The cells look bigger, and he can see more of them

feedback.b: A higher-power lens magnifies more, so the cells look bigger, not smaller.
feedback.c: Changing to a higher-power lens increases magnification, so the cells look bigger.
feedback.d: When you zoom in, you see a smaller area of the slide, so fewer cells fit in the view.

hints: Think about zooming in on a photo on your phone.
What happens to how much of the picture you can see when you zoom in?
solution: The ×40 lens magnifies 10 times more than the ×4 lens, so each cell looks **bigger**. But the **field of view** (the area of the slide you can see) gets smaller, so **fewer cells** fit in the view. The image usually looks dimmer too.

prompt: A cell has a cell wall, a nucleus and a large permanent vacuole, but no chloroplasts. Which cell is it most likely to be?

options.text: A root hair cell from a plant
A cheek cell from a human
A palisade cell from a leaf
A red blood cell from a human

feedback.b: Cheek cells are animal cells, so they have no cell wall or large vacuole.
feedback.c: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
feedback.d: Red blood cells are animal cells with no cell wall. They also have no nucleus.

hints: The cell wall and large vacuole tell you it's a plant cell.
Which part of a plant gets no light?
solution: The cell wall and large vacuole show it is a **plant cell**. It has no chloroplasts, so it comes from a part of the plant that gets no light: a **root hair cell**.

prompt: Compare plant cells and animal cells. Give **two** similarities and **two** differences.
modelAnswer:
Similarities: both plant and animal cells have a nucleus, which contains DNA and controls the cell. Both have a cell membrane, which controls what enters and leaves the cell. (Both also have cytoplasm and mitochondria.)

Differences: plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, but animal cells do not. Plant cells have chloroplasts for photosynthesis, but animal cells do not. Plant cells also have a large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, which animal cells do not have.

rubric.criterion: Gives one correct similarity (both have a nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm or mitochondria)
Gives a second, different correct similarity
Gives one correct difference (only plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large permanent vacuole)
Gives a second, different correct difference

hints: List the structures found in both kinds of cell, then the ones found only in plant cells.
For a difference, say which cell has the structure and which doesn't.
solution:
| Structure | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cell membrane | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cytoplasm | ✓ | ✓ |
| Mitochondria | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cell wall | ✓ | ✗ |
| Chloroplasts | ✓ (in green parts) | ✗ |
| Large permanent vacuole | ✓ | ✗ |

Any two shared structures are similarities. Any two plant-only structures are differences, as long as you say that animal cells don't have them.

prompt: A student's drawing of a plant cell is 50 mm long. The drawing has a magnification of ×250. What is the actual length of the cell in micrometres (µm)?
hints: Rearrange the formula: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
Your first answer will be in millimetres. 1 mm = 1000 µm.
solution:
Actual size = image size ÷ magnification $= 50 \div 250 = 0.2$ mm.

Convert to micrometres: $0.2 \times 1000 = 200$ µm.

The cell is **200 µm** long.

prompt: In Aroha's photo, a cheek cell is 40 mm wide. She knows the real cell is 80 µm wide. She works out 40 ÷ 80 = 0.5 and writes "magnification ×0.5". What went wrong?

options.text: She didn't put both sizes in the same units. 40 mm = 40 000 µm, so the magnification is ×500.
She divided the wrong way round. It should be 80 ÷ 40, so the magnification is ×2.
She should have multiplied the two sizes, so the magnification is ×3200.
Nothing went wrong. A magnification below ×1 is normal for photos of cells.

feedback.b: The formula is image size ÷ actual size, so she divided the right way round. Her mistake was mixing mm and µm.
feedback.c: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. You never multiply the two sizes.
feedback.d: A magnification below ×1 would mean the photo is smaller than the real cell. A 40 mm photo of a tiny cell must be magnified a lot.

hints: Look at the units of each measurement.
solution: Both sizes must be in the same units. $40 \text{ mm} = 40\,000\ \mu\text{m}$, so the magnification $= 40\,000 \div 80 = 500$. The photo is magnified **×500**.

prompt: Name the flat part of a microscope that the slide sits on.
hints: It usually has two clips to hold the slide in place.
solution: The slide sits on the **stage**, held in place by clips. Light shines up through a hole in the stage.
